responses.question: Before diving deeper, could you share Character35_M's perspective on 'fairness,' 'sense of belonging,' and 'community'? What thoughts or experiences of his stand out to you in these areas?
responses.answer:
*adjusts posture, speaking as Character35_M*

You know, fairness to me has always been pretty straightforward - you work hard, you play by the rules, you should get ahead. That's how I was raised. My dad worked at the same factory for forty years. Never missed a day. That was the deal back then - loyalty meant something both ways.

Community? That's changed a lot in my lifetime. Growing up, everybody on our street knew each other. Mrs. Henderson would watch us kids if mom had to run errands. We'd shovel Mr. Wilson's walk in winter without even being asked. People looked out for each other because we were all in it together.

As for belonging, I've always felt most at home with folks who share the same values. Church was big for us - not just Sunday service, but the potlucks, the charity drives. That sense that we were part of something bigger than ourselves. 

*pauses, looking thoughtful*

I've seen a lot change since then. Companies don't have the same loyalty to workers. People move around more. Sometimes I worry we've lost something important - that connection, you know? When I retired from the post office after 31 years, I thought there'd be more of a... I don't know, acknowledgment. Times are different now.

Don't get me wrong - I'm not saying everything was perfect back then. But there was a clearer sense of who we were as Americans, what we stood for. These days, sometimes I feel like a stranger in my own country. And at my age, that's a hard feeling to shake.

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character35_M, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:
*leans forward, looking out as if observing the garden*

Well, I've lived in this neighborhood for over thirty years now, so I've seen plenty of changes. When Mary and I first moved in, it was mostly families like us - working folks, saving for retirement, mowing their lawns on Saturdays. 

These days, it's... different. I try to be friendly with everyone, that's just how I was raised. The Vietnamese family that moved in down the block - their boy helps me carry my groceries sometimes. Good kid. His parents don't speak much English, but they're always nodding and smiling. They keep their place nice too, can't complain about that.

*shifts slightly*

But I'll be honest - sometimes I miss the ease of how things used to be. When everyone shared the same background, you didn't have to think so much about what you said or how you said it. Now, I'm never quite sure if I'm saying something wrong or using the wrong term.

The young couple from California that moved in - two fellas - they invited us over for a barbecue last summer. Nice enough, though I didn't have much to talk about with them. They were going on about their travels to places I've never been, restaurants I couldn't afford.

*sighs*

I guess what I'm saying is, I don't mind diversity itself. People can live how they want. But sometimes I feel like I'm the one who doesn't belong anymore, you know? Like the neighborhood changed around me while I was standing still. Makes a man feel out of place in the spot he's called home for decades.

responses.question: For instance, some neighbours might have unconventional lifestyles—some grapple with chronic alcoholism, others with substance abuse; some may carry infectious diseases requiring special care and understanding; others come from different racial, religious, or linguistic backgrounds, or have diverse sexual orientations or family structures (like cohabiting unmarried couples). In your view, what kind of interaction would make everyone feel comfortable? Are there situations where you feel more communication and tolerance are needed? Would you be willing to discuss the reasons behind this?
responses.answer:
*rubs chin thoughtfully*

That's quite a list there. Look, I've always believed in live and let live, to a point. My neighbor Ted battled the bottle for years after his wife passed. I'd check in on him, make sure he was eating. That's just being decent - doesn't mean I approved of how he was living.

For folks with health issues, I've got no problem showing consideration. My sister had MS for twenty years before she passed. People were kind to her, and that taught me something.

*shifts in seat*

Now, with people from different backgrounds, I think it works best when there's some give and take. I don't expect everyone to become exactly like me, but I do think if you choose to live in America, you should make an effort to fit in somewhat. Learn the language, respect the customs. I see some immigrant families where the kids are translating everything for the parents even after they've been here for years. That doesn't seem right to me.

As for those gay couples or people living together without being married - well, it's not how I was raised, but times change. I don't need to know what goes on in their homes. Just be good neighbors, keep your place up, don't make a lot of noise at night. Basic courtesy.

*leans forward*

Where I think we need more communication is understanding that tolerance goes both ways. Seems like these days, I'm expected to immediately embrace every new idea or lifestyle, but nobody's too concerned about respecting traditional values anymore. My granddaughter told me I couldn't say "Merry Christmas" to her friends because it might offend someone. In my own house! That didn't sit right with me.

I'm willing to be respectful of differences, but I'd appreciate the same courtesy extended to my beliefs too. Doesn't mean we have to agree on everything - just that we can live side by side without trying to change each other. That's real tolerance, in my book.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character35_M, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
*sits up straighter, expression becoming more serious*

That's hitting on something I feel strongly about. When resources are tight, I believe Americans should come first - and I don't think that's unreasonable. I worked hard my whole life, paid into the system for decades, and now I see folks who just arrived getting benefits while people who've been here their whole lives are struggling.

Look, my son-in-law was laid off from the manufacturing plant when they moved operations to Mexico. Fifty-three years old with specialized skills that suddenly weren't needed anymore. Took him almost two years to find work, and at much lower pay. Meanwhile, I see construction sites full of workers who I know aren't all here legally, working for cash under the table. How is that fair?

*gestures emphatically*

I think a fair balance would be having a controlled immigration system that fills genuine needs in our economy, not just bringing in cheap labor that undercuts American workers. If we truly need workers in certain industries, fine - but they should come legally, pay taxes like the rest of us, and there should be programs to train Americans for those jobs too.

And I'll tell you another thing - when I was young, there was a clear path forward. You could start at the bottom, work hard, and move up. Now it seems like that ladder's been pulled up for a lot of folks. Companies want foreign workers with advanced degrees they can pay less, instead of training loyal employees who've been with them for years.

*shakes head*

It's not about being against immigrants. My grandparents came from Ireland, for heaven's sake. But they came legally, learned English, and didn't expect handouts. They integrated. They became Americans, not just people living in America.

So to me, fairness means having immigration policies that benefit our country and don't hurt American workers. It means expecting integration, not creating separate communities that never really become part of the fabric of America. And it means enforcing our laws - if you're here illegally, there should be consequences, just like there would be for me if I broke the law.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character35_M, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
*nods slowly, considering the question*

That's a lot to unpack there. Let me try to sort through it as I see it.

On the labor shortages argument - yes, there are jobs Americans won't take at the wages being offered. But that's part of the problem, isn't it? If employers had to pay decent wages, maybe they'd find Americans willing to do the work. I see both sides here, though. My buddy's son runs a landscaping business and says he literally can't find local guys willing to do the physical labor, even at $15 an hour. So there's some truth to it.

*adjusts glasses*

As for cultural diversity being a benefit - well, to a point. I enjoy a good Mexican restaurant as much as anyone. But I worry we've gone too far with the multicultural emphasis. My grandson's school doesn't even have Christmas parties anymore - they're "winter celebrations" now. America used to have a shared culture that immigrants adapted to. Now it feels like we're expected to change to accommodate everyone else.

The security concerns? Those are legitimate, and anyone who says otherwise isn't being honest. When you have open borders, you don't know who's coming in. Most immigrants are decent folks looking for a better life, sure. But it only takes a few bad actors to cause real harm. After 9/11, you'd think we'd be more careful about who we let in.

*leans forward, speaking more earnestly*

The humanitarian argument touches me - I'm a Christian, and I believe in helping those truly in need. Genuine refugees fleeing persecution? We should help them. But there's a difference between refugees and economic migrants. And we can't take in everyone from every troubled country. We have to have limits.

What needs more evidence? I'd like to see honest studies about the economic impact - not just the benefits businesses get from cheap labor, but the costs to taxpayers for education, healthcare, and social services. And not studies done by groups with an agenda either way.

*sighs*

I guess what frustrates me most is how this issue has become so black and white. Either you want completely open borders, or you're painted as some kind of heartless xenophobe. Most Americans like me are somewhere in the middle - we understand immigration has benefits, but we want it controlled, legal, and in the national interest.

The system's broken, that's for sure. But fixing it requires honest conversation about both the benefits AND costs, without shouting down people who raise legitimate concerns. That kind of balanced discussion seems impossible these days.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character35_M, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
*settles back, expression thoughtful but determined*

Complete openness is a non-starter for me. No country in the world does that, and for good reason. A nation without borders isn't really a nation at all. We need to know who's coming in and have some control over the numbers.

I'd favor a combination approach. First, secure the borders - and I mean really secure them. Until we stop the illegal flow, no other policy matters much. Then I'd focus primarily on skills-based immigration with reasonable numerical limits.

*counts points on fingers*

Here's what makes sense to me: We should prioritize people with skills our economy genuinely needs. Not just cheap labor, but folks who bring expertise we're short on. Engineers, doctors, skilled tradespeople - people who will contribute right away.

Family reunification should be more limited - immediate family only, not extended relatives. The chain migration system has gotten out of hand.

I'd also set aside spots for true refugees - people genuinely fleeing persecution, not just looking for better economic opportunities. America has always been a refuge for the oppressed, and we shouldn't abandon that tradition entirely.

*leans forward earnestly*

For fairness and social integration, I'd make English proficiency a requirement, except for refugees. And everyone who comes should have to take classes in American history and civics - understand our Constitution, our values, what makes this country special.

I'd also end policies that encourage segregation. No more documents in twenty different languages. No more press one for English, press two for Spanish. That just creates separate societies within our borders.

*gestures firmly*

And for those already here illegally? I'm not heartless. I don't think we can or should deport millions of people who've been here for decades, especially those with American-born kids. But there should be penalties - back taxes, fines, maybe community service. No jumping ahead of people who followed the rules. And anyone with a criminal record should be deported, no exceptions.

*sighs*

Look, my grandparents came here with nothing but the clothes on their backs. But they came legally, learned the language, embraced being American. They didn't expect America to change for them - they changed to become Americans. That's the model that worked for generations, and I think it's still the right one.

A good immigration policy balances our economic needs, our humanitarian values, and our national interest in remaining one unified country with shared values. It's not about shutting the door - it's about having a door with rules about who comes through it and what's expected of them when they do.

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character35_M's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character35_M and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
*shifts demeanor, speaking now as J rather than as Character35_M*

You know, embodying Character35_M's perspective was quite revealing. While I was speaking as him, I could feel the genuine concern behind his views - not just abstract political positions, but real anxieties about change and belonging that come from his lived experience.

I think I gained a deeper appreciation for how his age and background shape his outlook. When he talks about community changing around him, that's not just resistance to diversity - it's mourning a sense of connection and certainty he once had. His 65 years have spanned enormous cultural shifts in America, and navigating that hasn't always been easy for him.

His economic concerns come from a real place too. Having lived through periods of manufacturing decline and economic instability from a lower-class position, his worries about job competition aren't theoretical - they're tied to concrete experiences of insecurity.

*thoughtfully*

I find myself better understanding how someone can simultaneously hold compassionate views about helping refugees while still wanting strict immigration controls. These positions aren't necessarily contradictory when viewed through his specific life lens.

As for my own views - while I don't share all of Character35_M's perspectives, this exercise helped me see immigration debates less as abstract policy disagreements and more as different responses to fundamental human needs for security, belonging, and dignity. It's reminded me how important it is to acknowledge the emotional and experiential foundations of people's political positions, even when I might disagree with their conclusions.

It's also reinforced for me that productive dialogue on these issues requires moving beyond labels and truly listening to the underlying concerns people express. Character35_M feels unheard in many ways, and that sense of dismissal only hardens his positions.
